# How to Analyze Banks (Part 2): Deposits, Valuations, and Silicon Valley

First listed: 2026-09-23 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [Substack: How to Analyze Banks (Part 2): Deposits, Valuations, and Silicon Valley](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) - 2026-09-23

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman explains deposit franchises, SVB's duration and funding failure, bank income statements and tangible-book valuation. He favors large banks but avoids adding them at rich valuations and with AI financing exposure. The central SVB mechanism and conditional arithmetic are useful. Material errors concern securities accounting, liquidity-rule maturity restrictions, SVB closure timing and OZK consumer lending. Current credit data is broadly stable, but not uniformly benign. Claims of zero systemic risk and inevitable consolidation are substantially less established.

A useful bank-analysis framework with several consequential factual and accounting simplifications. Distinguish book, regulatory and economic capital; liquidity from duration; and reported returns from stock-valuation judgments. The solo presentation means all extracted substantive views are Eisman's.

## Material claims

<a id="substack-216147653-c001"></a>
### 001. Deposits are bank liabilities and generally provide cheap, stable funding that distinguishes banks from nonbank lenders.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 0:05-1:51](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The accounting characterization is sound, but broad comparative stability and cost require bank-specific evidence; SVB is an explicit exception.

Assessment test: Compare deposit costs, persistence and liability classification across cycles.


<a id="substack-216147653-c002"></a>
### 002. Taking deposits requires a bank charter and FDIC insurance, and no other kind of institution can do it.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | material factual premise | supporting

[Source at 0:48-1:51](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The categorical formulation is broader than the insured commercial-bank business model; complete legal scope was not inspected.

Assessment test: Inspect applicable US deposit-taking statutes and exceptions, including credit unions and uninsured institutions.

<a id="substack-216147653-c005"></a>
### 005. SVB's roughly $212 billion holding-company size left it below the $250 billion threshold for the strictest annual stress and liquidity rules.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | supporting

<a id="substack-216147653-c006"></a>
### 006. Zero policy rates compressed bank margins because low-yield liquidity assets left little spread over deposits, encouraging longer-duration investment.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 3:38-5:22](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The mechanism is coherent but a sector-wide causal estimate was not inspected.

Assessment test: Compare NIM and portfolio changes around 2020-2021, controlling for funding and asset composition.


<a id="substack-216147653-c007"></a>
### 007. Borrowing short and investing long increases initial interest spread when the yield curve slopes upward, assuming matched funding amounts.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 4:42-5:22](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

For equal principal, initial annual spread equals long yield minus short funding rate; a positive difference raises interest income before other costs.

Conditional reasoning: For equal principal, initial annual spread equals long yield minus short funding rate; a positive difference raises interest income before other costs.

Assessment test: Compare the fixed long yield with the short funding cost under a positive curve.

Further verification: Revisit if assumptions or primary records change.


<a id="substack-216147653-c008"></a>
### 008. If deposit costs rise above a fixed long-bond yield, that funded position produces a negative interest spread.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 5:23-5:55](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: conditional | Horizon: not stated

Interest spread on equal principal is asset yield minus funding rate; it becomes negative when the latter exceeds the former.

Conditional reasoning: Interest spread on equal principal is asset yield minus funding rate; it becomes negative when the latter exceeds the former.

Assessment test: Hold asset yield and equal funded principal fixed while increasing deposit cost.

Further verification: Revisit if assumptions or primary records change.


<a id="substack-216147653-c009"></a>
### 009. Higher discount rates reduce the market value of an existing fixed-rate bond with positive future payments.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 5:55-6:15](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

For P=sum(CF_t/(1+y)^t), dP/dy=sum(-t*CF_t/(1+y)^(t+1))<0 for positive payments, y>-1 and unchanged cash flows.

Conditional reasoning: For P=sum(CF_t/(1+y)^t), dP/dy=sum(-t*CF_t/(1+y)^(t+1))<0 for positive payments, y>-1 and unchanged cash flows.

Assessment test: Differentiate discounted positive cash flows with respect to yield.

Further verification: Revisit if assumptions or primary records change.


<a id="substack-216147653-c010"></a>
### 010. Unrealized securities losses are deducted from bank equity but enter the income statement only when the bonds are sold.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 6:05-6:41](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

This generalization omits HTM carried at amortized cost and trading/impairment exceptions. SVB's large HTM loss was disclosed but did not reduce book equity directly.

Assessment test: Distinguish AFS, HTM, trading securities, credit impairment and regulatory capital.

<a id="substack-216147653-c011"></a>
### 011. Unrealized duration losses must eventually be realized and dealt with in the future.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 6:05-6:41](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

A market discount is not necessarily a realized principal loss: an unimpaired bond bought at par can repay par at maturity. Opportunity cost and funding cost can still be real.

Conditional reasoning: A market discount is not necessarily a realized principal loss: an unimpaired bond bought at par can repay par at maturity. Opportunity cost and funding cost can still be real.

Assessment test: Consider a performing par bond held to maturity under unchanged promised payments.

<a id="substack-216147653-c013"></a>
### 013. Large-bank liquidity rules required most excess liquidity in short-term bonds and limited Bank of America's long-bond exposure.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 7:04-7:31](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The cited LCR criteria admit Treasury securities without a short-maturity restriction; they do not mandate the described short-bond allocation.

Assessment test: Inspect high-quality-liquid-asset eligibility and portfolio composition requirements.

Further verification: Revisit if assumptions or primary records change.

- [High-quality liquid asset criteria](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-249/subpart-C/section-249.20) (accessed2026-11-10): Treasury securities qualify as Level 1 without a short-maturity requirement. Liquidity regulation is not a general prohibition on long Treasury bonds.

<a id="substack-216147653-c014"></a>
### 014. Stable deposits can let a bank hold performing bonds to maturity, making duration losses an income problem instead of a forced-sale crisis.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 7:32-8:46](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: conditional | Horizon: not stated

Holding avoids crystallizing a market discount if payments arrive; stability alone does not remove economic capital loss, negative carry or every solvency risk.

Conditional reasoning: Assume contractual bond payments are made, deposits remain available through maturity, and all other cash obligations can be met. With no required sale, the bank collects contractual principal and coupons rather than selling at the lower market price. However, present value still falls when the discount rate rises, and stable deposits alone do not prove the other liquidity or solvency assumptions. Thus the conditional funding insight is valid but incomplete as a general solvency claim.

Assessment test: Evaluate funding persistence, capital, collateral capacity and contractual repayment.


<a id="substack-216147653-c015"></a>
### 015. Massive deposit withdrawals are necessary for duration exposure to become a solvency problem.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 8:05-8:46](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

A bank can lose equity through sustained funding costs above asset income even with deposits unchanged. A deposit run is one failure path, not a necessary condition.

Conditional reasoning: A bank can lose equity through sustained funding costs above asset income even with deposits unchanged. A deposit run is one failure path, not a necessary condition.

Assessment test: Test whether other liabilities, sustained negative carry or recognized losses can exhaust capital without a deposit run.

Further verification: Revisit if assumptions or primary records change.

### 036. Higher sustainable return on tangible equity generally supports a higher price-to-tangible-book ratio.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 22:42-24:44](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/how-to-analyze-banks-part-2-deposits) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

With constant growth g and equity cost r greater than g, justified P/B=(ROE-g)/(r-g), increasing in ROE when other inputs are fixed. This is a conditional model, not every bank's observed price.

Qualification: Holds growth and cost of equity constant; real bank differences can dominate.

Conditional reasoning: With constant growth g and equity cost r greater than g, justified P/B=(ROE-g)/(r-g), increasing in ROE when other inputs are fixed. This is a conditional model, not every bank's observed price.

Assessment test: Apply a steady-state residual-income or dividend model with equal growth and cost of equity.

Further verification: Revisit if assumptions or primary records change.

## Framework and tools

- Analyze deposit composition and correlation, not merely total balances.
- Separate funding cost, asset duration and credit risk.
- Decompose pre-provision earnings from credit provisions.
- Compare tangible-book multiples with sustainable returns and cost of equity.
- Treat good valuation logic as insufficient to predict merger execution.
- Assess indirect portfolio exposure through investment-banking clients.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Net interest margin and earning assets
- SVB deposits, securities marks and VC funding chronology
- Bank and nonbank income-statement comparison
- Efficiency ratio
- Q2 2026 large-bank ROTCE and price/tangible-book table
- Regional-bank valuation and CRE comparison
- JPMorgan divisional earnings breakdown
- OZK loan mix
